page: Vultr vhf-4c-16gb is a virtual server belonging to the High Frequency Compute family. It features an x86_64 Intel processor with 4 shared vCPUs, mapped from 2 physical cores with hyperthreading enabled. The system is configured with 16.0 GB of memory, providing 4.0 GB per core, and includes a bundled 384 GB NVMe SSD for local storage. It does not include any GPU hardware.

Performance benchmarks indicate average single-core and multi-core capabilities, with a stress-ng single-core score of 2411.16 and a multi-core score of 8740.87. While cached small-block memory read bandwidth is strong at 497.33 GB/sec, uncached large-block read and write speeds are weaker, measuring 35.47 GB/sec and 17.49 GB/sec respectively. Computational tasks like software compilation and image processing fall into the lower performance tier, as evidenced by a Geekbench multi-core score of 4280.0 and a Clang compilation score of 5746.0.

Given its shared CPU allocation and moderate memory-to-core ratio, this server offers a cost-efficient entry point for workloads that do not require dedicated CPU threads. It is suitable for general-purpose tasks, basic web serving, text processing, and lightweight single-threaded applications. However, it is less optimal for heavy database operations, parallelized decompression, or medium-to-large language model inference due to its lower multi-core efficiency and uncached memory bandwidth constraints.
description: Vultr vhf-4c-16gb is a general-purpose virtual server in the High Frequency Compute family, featuring 4 shared Intel vCPUs (2 physical cores with hyperthreading) and 16.0 GB of RAM. The server includes a bundled 384 GB NVMe SSD for local storage but lacks GPU acceleration. Benchmark results show average single-core performance, with a Geekbench single-core score of 1471.0, but weaker multi-core scaling and uncached memory bandwidth. This hardware profile is qualitatively cost-efficient for workloads requiring moderate memory and local storage without sustained, dedicated CPU performance. It is best suited for general-purpose applications, text processing, and lightweight web serving, while being less optimal for database operations or intensive multi-threaded compilation.
